skills.name: benchmarking
skills.description: Guide for building, running, and analyzing Nanvix performance benchmarks. Use this when asked about benchmark setup, execution, or interpretation.

skills.name: build
skills.description: Guide for building, formatting, linting, and spell-checking Nanvix with z. Use this when asked to build or validate the repository.

skills.name: ci-cd-pipeline
skills.description: Guide for Nanvix CI and GitHub Actions workflow behavior, including local pipeline execution and matrix coverage. Use this when asked about CI checks, workflow failures, or release flow.

skills.name: coding-standards
skills.description: Detailed Nanvix coding, documentation, and review standards across Rust, C/C++, Python, and Shell. Use this when asked to implement or review code quality conventions.

skills.name: daemon-development
skills.description: Guide for developing and debugging Nanvix daemons, including guest daemons and host linuxd behavior. Use this when asked about daemon architecture or daemon changes.

skills.name: gdb-debugging
skills.description: Guide for debugging Nanvix guests using GDB remote debugging over the microvm machine type. Use this when asked about attaching GDB, setting breakpoints, or stepping through kernel code.

skills.name: kernel-development
skills.description: Guide for modifying and debugging the Nanvix kernel architecture and kernel-call paths. Use this when asked about kernel internals or kernel implementation changes.

skills.name: library-development
skills.description: Guide for creating and modifying Nanvix libraries under src/libs, including guest no_std and host std crates. Use this when asked about library architecture or crate changes.

skills.name: test-development
skills.description: Guide for writing, running, and debugging Nanvix unit, integration, and system tests in Rust and C/C++. Use this when asked about test implementation or failures.

skills.name: test
skills.description: Guide for running Nanvix tests with z. Use this when asked to run unit tests, integration tests, or the full test suite.

skills.name: troubleshooting
skills.description: Guide for diagnosing Nanvix build, runtime, and test failures, including cleanup and debugging workflows. Use this when asked to investigate errors or unstable behavior.

skills.name: user-app-development
skills.description: Guide for developing, building, and running Nanvix user-space applications across supported runtimes and languages. Use this when asked about guest app implementation or execution.

skills.name: find-skills
skills.description: Helps users discover and install agent skills when they ask questions like "how do I do X", "find a skill for X", "is there a skill that can...", or express interest in extending capabilities. This skill should be used when the user is looking for functionality that might exist as an installable skill.

skills.name: customize-cloud-agent
skills.description: Skill for customizing the Copilot cloud agent (formerly known as Copilot coding agent) environment, including copilot-setup-steps.yml configuration, preinstalling tools and dependencies, runners, and settings. Use when the user mentions copilot-setup-steps, copilot setup steps, or wants to configure the cloud agent environment.

1. // Copyright(c) The Maintainers of Nanvix.
2. // Licensed under the MIT License.
3. 
4. //==================================================================================================
5. // Imports
6. //==================================================================================================
7. 
8. use vstd::prelude::*;
9. #[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
10. include!("table.spec.rs");
11. #[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
12. include!("table.proof.rs");
13. 
14. use super::{
15.     PteWord,
16.     PTE_WORD_SIZE_LOG2,
17. };
18. 
19. //==================================================================================================
20. // Table Entry Trait
21. //==================================================================================================
22. 
23. ///
24. /// # Description
25. ///
26. /// Trait bound for entry types that can be stored in a page table.
27. ///
28. /// The raw representation uses [`PteWord`] — `u32` on x86.
29. ///
30. pub trait TableEntry: Copy {
31.     /// Creates from a raw [`PteWord`], returning `None` if the value is invalid.
32.     fn from_raw(raw: PteWord) -> Option<Self>;
33.     /// Returns the raw [`PteWord`] representation.
34.     fn raw(self) -> PteWord;
35. }
36. 
37. //==================================================================================================
38. // Table Index
39. //==================================================================================================
40. 
41. ///
42. /// # Description
43. ///
44. /// A validated index into a page table, guaranteed to be in `[0, PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH)`.
45. ///
46. #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
47. pub struct TableIndex(usize);
48. 
49. impl TableIndex {
50.     ///
51.     /// # Description
52.     ///
53.     /// Creates a [`TableIndex`] from a raw `usize`, returning `None` if the value is out of
54.     /// bounds.
55.     ///
56.     pub const fn new(index: usize) -> Option<Self> {
57.         if index < crate::mem::PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH {
58.             Some(Self(index))
59.         } else {
60.             None
61.         }
62.     }
63. 
64.     ///
65.     /// # Description
66.     ///
67.     /// Returns the underlying index value.
68.     ///
69.     pub const fn into_raw(self) -> usize {
70.         self.0
71.     }
72. }
73. 
74. //==================================================================================================
75. // Virtual Address Index Extraction
76. //==================================================================================================
77. 
78. /// Extracts the PD index (bits 22-31) from a virtual address as a [`TableIndex`].
79. pub const fn pd_index(vaddr: usize) -> TableIndex {
80.     // The mask guarantees the result is always < PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH.
81.     let index: usize = (vaddr >> crate::mem::PGTAB_SHIFT) & (crate::mem::PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH - 1);
82.     TableIndex(index)
83. }
84. 
85. /// Extracts the PT index (bits 12-21) from a virtual address as a [`TableIndex`].
86. pub const fn pt_index(vaddr: usize) -> TableIndex {
87.     // The mask guarantees the result is always < PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH.
88.     let index: usize = (vaddr >> crate::mem::PAGE_SHIFT) & (crate::mem::PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH - 1);
89.     TableIndex(index)
90. }
91. 
92. //==================================================================================================
93. // Table
94. //==================================================================================================
95. 
96. ///
97. /// # Description
98. ///
99. /// A page-table page containing [`PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH`](crate::mem::PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH) entries.
100. ///
101. /// This type is parameterized over the entry type to enforce that each table level uses only
102. /// its own entry kind (e.g., PD tables only [`PageDirectoryEntry`], PT tables only
103. /// [`PageTableEntry`]).
104. ///
105. /// The table is accessed via a base address that must be valid in the current address space
106. /// (i.e., a mapped virtual address). It does not own the backing memory — the caller is
107. /// responsible for allocation and lifetime management.
108. ///
109. #[derive(Debug)]
110. pub struct Table<E: TableEntry> {
111.     /// Base address of the table (must be page-aligned).
112.     base: usize,
113.     /// Phantom marker for the entry type.
114.     _marker: ::core::marker::PhantomData<E>,
115. }
116. 
117. impl<E: TableEntry> Table<E> {
118.     ///
119.     /// # Description
120.     ///
121.     /// Creates a table reference from a base address.
122.     ///
123.     /// # Safety
124.     ///
125.     /// `base` must be a valid, page-aligned address with at least one page of readable/writable
126.     /// memory.
127.     ///
128.     pub const unsafe fn from_address(base: usize) -> Self {
129.         Self {
130.             base,
131.             _marker: ::core::marker::PhantomData,
132.         }
133.     }
134. 
135.     ///
136.     /// # Description
137.     ///
138.     /// Reads the entry at `index`.
139.     ///
140.     /// Returns `None` if the raw value is invalid according to `E::from_raw()`.
141.     ///
142.     /// # Safety
143.     ///
144.     /// The memory at `base + index * size_of::<PteWord>()` must be valid for a volatile read.
145.     ///
146.     pub unsafe fn read(&self, index: TableIndex) -> Option<E> {
147.         let offset: usize = index.into_raw() << PTE_WORD_SIZE_LOG2;
148.         let ptr: *const PteWord = (self.base + offset) as *const PteWord;
149.         E::from_raw(::core::ptr::read_volatile(ptr))
150.     }
151. 
152.     ///
153.     /// # Description
154.     ///
155.     /// Writes `entry` at `index`.
156.     ///
157.     /// # Safety
158.     ///
159.     /// The memory at `base + index * size_of::<PteWord>()` must be valid for a volatile write.
160.     ///
161.     pub unsafe fn write(&self, index: TableIndex, entry: E) {
162.         let offset: usize = index.into_raw() << PTE_WORD_SIZE_LOG2;
163.         let ptr: *mut PteWord = (self.base + offset) as *mut PteWord;
164.         ::core::ptr::write_volatile(ptr, entry.raw());
165.     }
166. }
167.

1. # Caller Analysis: `arch::x86::mem::paging::table`
2. 
3. ## Script Output
4. 
5. Raw `find_callers_lsp.py` output reported **7 public exec functions, 0 private,
6. 2 types (`Table`, `TableIndex`)** and — importantly — **0 external callers for
7. every public function** (only internal callers of `TableIndex::into_raw` from
8. `Table::read`/`Table::write`).
9. 
10. > **Why the script found 0 external callers (false negative).**
11. > This module lives under `src/libs/arch/src/x86/` — the **32-bit x86** build.
12. > rust-analyzer (and thus the script) indexes the **x86_64 host** configuration,
13. > so all real call sites — which are compiled only under `cfg(target_arch =
14. > "x86")` (kernel) or are host-side software page-walkers — are invisible to the
15. > LSP. A textual search across the workspace recovers the true callers below.
16. > Treat the script's "no external callers" warning as a configuration artifact,
17. > **not** as evidence of dead code.
18. 
19. In-scope (verification-order) functions: `Table::write`, `TableIndex::into_raw`,
20. `raw`, `Table::read`, `from_raw`, `pt_index`, `TableIndex`, `pd_index`,
21. `Table::from_address`. (`raw`/`from_raw` are the `TableEntry` trait methods,
22. implemented in `pde.rs`/`pte.rs` and dispatched only inside `Table::read`/`write`.)
23. 
24. ## Real Callers (recovered by source search)
25. 
26. ### 1. Kernel identity map — `src/kernel/src/mm/virt/identity_map.rs` (primary consumer)
27. 
28. This is the canonical user of the whole module. It walks/builds the kernel's
29. two-level identity map:
30. 
31. - `paging::pd_index(vaddr)` / `paging::pt_index(vaddr)` → `TableIndex`
32.   (L131, L306, L728, L729, L783, L848).
33. - `unsafe { Table::<PageDirectoryEntry>::from_address(pd_paddr) }` and
34.   `Table::<PageTableEntry>::from_address(pt_paddr)` to obtain a typed view over a
35.   physical (identity-mapped) page (L133, L297, L299, L732, L736, L785, L852, L863).
36. - `unsafe { pd.read(pde_idx) }` / `pt.read(pte_idx)` returning
37.   `Option<PageDirectoryEntry>` / `Option<PageTableEntry>`; callers treat `None`
38.   as "invalid entry" → `ErrorCode::InvalidArgument` (L308, L316, L535, L633,
39.   L786, L853, L864).
40. - `unsafe { pd.write(pde_idx, new_pde) }` / `pt.write(pte_idx, new_pte)` to
41.   install freshly-built entries (L320, L583, L665).
42. - The entry-type parameter `E` is fixed per level: PD tables only carry
43.   `PageDirectoryEntry`, PT tables only `PageTableEntry`. The phantom-typed
44.   `Table<E>` is exactly what enforces this at the call sites.
45. 
46. ### 2. UserVM guest page walker — `src/uservm/src/guest_profiler/gva.rs` (host-side)
47. 
48. `translate_gva()` performs a *software* two-level walk over guest memory:
49. 
50. ```rust
51. let pd_index: usize = paging::pd_index(gva as usize).into_raw();
52. let pt_index: usize = paging::pt_index(gva as usize).into_raw();
53. ```
54. 
55. Here only `pd_index`/`pt_index` and `TableIndex::into_raw` are used; the table
56. bytes are read directly from a host pointer (`read_unaligned`) rather than via
57. `Table::read`, because the guest's memory is not mapped into the host address
58. space. This caller relies *solely* on the index-extraction arithmetic being
59. correct (mask to `[0, PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH)`) and on `into_raw` returning that same
60. value unchanged.
61. 
62. ## Pre-existing Specs (from upstream verification)
63. 
64. - **Source:** added while verifying the kernel `mm::virt::identity_map` module.
65. - **File:** `src/kernel/src/mm/virt/identity_map.spec.rs`.
66. - These are **trusted external boundary specs** for this not-yet-verified module:
67.   - `#[verifier::external_type_specification] #[external_body]` for
68.     `Table<E>` (`ExTable`) and `TableIndex` (`ExTableIndex`) — both opaque.

70.     `: Copy`).

74. - Functions WITHOUT specs: `TableIndex::new`, `TableIndex::into_raw`,
75.   and the `TableEntry::raw`/`from_raw` trait methods (no external spec; opaque).

78. ### Assessment

81.   given boundary specs; `into_raw`/`new` and the `raw`/`from_raw` trait methods
82.   are unspecified.

89.   `TableIndex → Option<E>` so that `read` after `write` can be reasoned about —

93. ## Trait Obligations

96.   - `from_raw(raw) -> Option<Self>`: parse a raw `PteWord` (`u32`), returning
97.     `None` exactly for raw values that are not a valid encoding of `E`.
98.   - `raw(self) -> PteWord`: serialize back to the raw word.
99.   - Round-trip expectation from callers: an entry built via `E::new(...)` and
100.     written, then read back, must yield `Some(equivalent entry)`; an
101.     all-zero / not-present word read by the identity map is a *valid* entry
102.     (returns `Some`, with `is_present() == false`) — `None` denotes structural
103.     corruption, which callers surface as `InvalidArgument`.
104.   - `Copy` lets `write` take `entry` by value and `read` return it freely.
105. 
106. ## Caller Expectations
107. 
108. ### `pd_index(vaddr) -> TableIndex`
109. - Callers assume: returns the PD index = `(vaddr >> PGTAB_SHIFT) &
110.   (PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH - 1)`, always in `[0, PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH)`. Total (no panic,
111.   no failure) for any `usize`. `const`.
112. - Callers don't care about: how the bits are masked, or that the result wraps an
113.   internal `usize` — only that `into_raw()` of it equals the masked value.
114. 
115. ### `pt_index(vaddr) -> TableIndex`
116. - Callers assume: returns the PT index = `(vaddr >> PAGE_SHIFT) &
117.   (PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH - 1)`, always in range; total; `const`.
118. - Callers don't care about: internal representation.
119. 
120. ### `TableIndex` (type) / `TableIndex::into_raw(self) -> usize`
121. - Callers assume: a `TableIndex` is a *validated* index, guaranteed
122.   `< PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH`; `into_raw` is the identity projection back to that
123.   validated `usize` (loss-less, total, `const`). `gva.rs` multiplies it by entry
124.   size with `checked_mul`, relying on the bound to stay within a page.
125. - Callers don't care about: that it is a newtype over `usize`; only the in-range
126.   invariant and the round-trip with the index extractors matter.
127. 
128. ### `Table::from_address(base) -> Table<E>` (`unsafe`, `const`)
129. - Callers assume: produces a typed, non-owning handle over the page at physical/
130.   identity-mapped `base`; cheap, infallible, side-effect-free. The caller carries
131.   the safety obligation (`base` page-aligned, mapped, readable/writable).
132. - Callers don't care about: that the struct stores only `base` + a `PhantomData`
133.   marker; they care that the phantom type `E` is threaded so PD/PT handles can't
134.   be confused.
135. 
136. ### `Table::read(&self, index) -> Option<E>` (`unsafe`)
137. - Callers assume: volatile-reads the word at `base + index*4` and decodes it via
138.   `E::from_raw`; `Some(e)` for a valid encoding, `None` for an invalid one. Does
139.   not mutate the table. The validated `index` guarantees in-bounds access.
140. - Callers don't care about: the volatile-read mechanism or the `<<
141.   PTE_WORD_SIZE_LOG2` offset math — only the index→entry mapping and the `None`
142.   = "invalid entry" contract (which they map to `InvalidArgument`).
143. 
144. ### `Table::write(&self, index, entry)` (`unsafe`)
145. - Callers assume: volatile-writes `entry.raw()` to `base + index*4`, so that a
146.   subsequent `read(index)` observes `Some(entry)` (read-after-write round-trip).
147.   Only the targeted slot changes. The validated `index` keeps the write in
148.   bounds of the page.
149. - Callers don't care about: the volatile mechanism or offset computation.
150. 
151. ### `TableEntry::from_raw` / `TableEntry::raw`
152. - No direct external callers; invoked only inside `read`/`write`. Expectation is
153.   the round-trip described under *Trait Obligations*.
154. 
155. ## Abstract Resource
156. 
157. This module manages a **single hardware page-table page** as a fixed-length array
158. of `PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH` typed entries, addressed by a *validated* in-range index
159. (`TableIndex`) and accessed by raw base address. Abstractly it is a partial map
160. `TableIndex → Option<E>` over volatile memory the caller owns, plus the pure
161. helpers that derive the PD/PT index of a virtual address.
162. 
163. ## Key Invariants (caller perspective)
164. 
165. - **Index validity:** every `TableIndex` (whether from `pd_index`, `pt_index`, or
166.   `new`) satisfies `into_raw() < PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH`; this bound is what keeps
167.   `read`/`write` (and `gva.rs`'s `checked_mul`) within one page.
168. - **Index extraction correctness:** `pd_index`/`pt_index` return exactly the
169.   masked/shifted bit-field of `vaddr`, and `into_raw` returns that same value.
170. - **Read/write round-trip:** `write(i, e)` followed by `read(i)` yields
171.   `Some(e')` with `e'` decoding-equivalent to `e`; writes touch only slot `i`.
172. - **Decode totality:** `read` returns `None` only for raw words that are not a
173.   valid `E` encoding; a not-present (zeroed) entry is a valid `Some`, not `None`.
174. - **Type discipline:** `Table<E>`'s phantom `E` prevents mixing PD and PT entries
175.   across table levels — a property callers depend on but that has no runtime cost.
176. - **Non-ownership:** `from_address` does not allocate or free; lifetime/validity
177.   of the backing page is the caller's responsibility (encoded as `unsafe`).

1. # View Design: `arch::x86::mem::paging::table`
2. 
3. ## Abstract Resource
4. 
5. To callers this module is **a single hardware page-table page**: a fixed-length
6. array of `PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH` (= 1024) typed entries, addressed by a *validated*
7. in-range index (`TableIndex`) and backed by volatile, caller-owned memory at a
8. physical/identity-mapped base address.
9. 
10. Abstractly it is a **partial map `index → Option<E>`** over one page, plus two
11. pure helpers (`pd_index`, `pt_index`) that extract the directory/table index of
12. a virtual address. The phantom type `E` keeps PD and PT pages from being mixed.
13. 
14. Two types need abstraction:
15. 
16. | Type | What it is to a caller |
17. |------|------------------------|
18. | `TableIndex` | a *validated* slot number, guaranteed `< PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH` |
19. | `Table<E>` | a typed, non-owning handle whose observable content is the per-slot entry map |
20. 
21. ---
22. 
23. ## View Structs
24. 
25. ### `TableIndex`
26. 
27. A `TableIndex` carries exactly one piece of caller-visible information: the
28. validated index value. Its abstract value is a single `nat`.
29. 
30. ```rust
31. impl View for TableIndex {
32.     type V = nat;
33.     // value returned by into_raw(); always < PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH (see inv)
34.     pub closed spec fn view(&self) -> nat;
35. }
36. ```
37. 
38. ### `Table<E>`
39. 
40. ```rust
41. pub struct TableView<E: TableEntry> {
42.     /// Physical/identity-mapped base address this handle denotes.
43.     /// Caller-meaningful identity: which page read/write act on.
44.     pub addr: nat,
45.     /// Logical contents: the entry a `read` would return for each valid slot.
46.     /// `entries[i] == None` means slot `i` holds a word that is not a valid
47.     /// encoding of `E`; `Some(e)` (including a not-present, zeroed entry) is a
48.     /// valid decode.
49.     pub entries: Map<nat, Option<E>>,
50. }
51. 
52. impl View for Table<E> {
53.     type V = TableView<E>;
54.     pub closed spec fn view(&self) -> TableView<E>;
55. }
56. ```
57. 
58. `E: TableEntry` is `Copy`; the trait supplies two pure spec projections used by
59. the transitions below (their `requires`/`ensures` are designed in the spec
60. phase; `raw`/`from_raw` are in verification scope, so these are *proven*, not
61. assumed):
62. 
63. ```rust
64. spec fn spec_raw(self: E) -> PteWord;              // serialize
65. spec fn spec_from_raw(w: PteWord) -> Option<E>;    // decode (None = invalid)
66. ```
67. 
68. with the round-trip **trait law** `spec_from_raw(e.spec_raw()) == Some(e)`.
69. 
70. ---
71. 
72. ## Well-formedness Invariants
73. 
74. ```rust
75. // TableIndex: the validated-range guarantee callers depend on.
76. pub open spec fn inv(&self) -> bool {     // on TableIndex
77.     self@ < PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH
78. }
79. ```
80. 
81. ```rust
82. impl<E: TableEntry> TableView<E> {
83.     pub open spec fn inv(self) -> bool {
84.         // exactly one page worth of slots, no more, no fewer
85.         &&& self.entries.dom() =~= Set::new(|i: nat| i < PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH)
86.         // a page-table page is page-aligned
87.         &&& self.addr % PAGE_SIZE == 0
88.     }
89. }
90. ```
91. 
92. The `Table` type-level `inv()` is `self@.inv()`.
93. 
94. ---
95. 
96. ## Spec Transition Functions
97. 
98. ### Pure index extractors (produce a `TableIndex` value = `nat`)
99. 
100. ```rust
101. pub open spec fn spec_table_index(vaddr: nat, shift: nat) -> nat {
102.     (vaddr >> shift) & (PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH - 1)        // low 10 bits after shift
103. }
104. pub open spec fn spec_pd_index(vaddr: nat) -> nat { spec_table_index(vaddr, PGTAB_SHIFT) }
105. pub open spec fn spec_pt_index(vaddr: nat) -> nat { spec_table_index(vaddr, PAGE_SHIFT) }
106. ```
107. 
108. - `pd_index(vaddr)` → `result@ == spec_pd_index(vaddr as nat)` (and `inv`, i.e.
109.   `result@ < PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH`, which follows from the mask).
110. - `pt_index(vaddr)` → `result@ == spec_pt_index(vaddr as nat)` (and `inv`).
111. - `TableIndex::into_raw(self)` → `result == self@` (identity projection).
112. - `TableIndex::new(i)` → `Some(t)` iff `i < PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH`, and then
113.   `t@ == i`; `None` otherwise. *(out of stated scope, but specifiable.)*
114. 
115. ### Handle creation
116. 
117. ```rust
118. // from_address only fixes identity; contents are pre-existing memory.
119. pub open spec fn spec_from_address(base: nat) -> /* addr field of */ nat { base }
120. ```
121. 
122. - `Table::from_address(base)` → `result@.addr == base`. `entries` are left
123.   unconstrained: they reflect whatever the backing page already holds.
124. 
125. ### Read / write (the `index → Option<E>` map)
126. 
127. ```rust
128. impl<E: TableEntry> TableView<E> {
129.     pub open spec fn spec_read(self, idx: nat) -> Option<E> {
130.         self.entries[idx]
131.     }
132.     pub open spec fn spec_write(self, idx: nat, entry: E) -> TableView<E> {
133.         TableView {
134.             entries: self.entries.insert(idx, E::spec_from_raw(entry.spec_raw())),
135.             ..self                              // frame: addr unchanged
136.         }
137.     }
138. }
139. ```
140. 
141. - `Table::read(&self, index)` → `result == self@.spec_read(index@)`
142.   (requires `index@ < PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH`, met by `TableIndex::inv`).
143. - `Table::write(&self, index, entry)` →
144.   `self@ == old(self)@.spec_write(index@, entry)` — only slot `index@` changes,
145.   `addr` and every other slot are preserved by `..self` / `insert`.
146. 
147. **Read-after-write** falls out directly:
148. `spec_read(spec_write(s, i, e), i) == spec_from_raw(e.spec_raw())`, and by the
149. trait round-trip law this is `Some(e)`. Writes to `j != i` leave slot `i`
150. untouched because `Map::insert` only alters the keyed slot.
151. 
152. ---
153. 
154. ## Design Rationale (per field, with substitution test)
155. 
156. > Substitution test: *if the implementation were rewritten with a different
157. > algorithm, would this field still make sense?*
158. 
159. ### `TableIndex@ : nat`
160. - **Why:** the only thing every caller asks of a `TableIndex` is its numeric
161.   value and the promise it is `< PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH`. `gva.rs` does
162.   `into_raw().checked_mul(entry_size)` relying on that bound; `identity_map.rs`
163.   feeds it straight to `read`/`write`.
164. - **Substitution:** ✅ Any representation (newtype over `usize`, a `u16`, a
165.   bitfield slice) still denotes one index value. `nat` is the algorithm-free
166.   essence; `into_raw` is its identity projection.
167. 
168. ### `TableView::addr : nat`
169. - **Why:** `from_address` has no other observable contract than *“this handle
170.   denotes the page at `base`.”* Callers build PD/PT handles from physical
171.   addresses they computed and must know the handle refers to that page.
172. - **Substitution:** ✅ Any handle to a page-table page must know which page it
173.   addresses, regardless of how it stores it. (The `PhantomData` marker, by
174.   contrast, is pure implementation and is excluded — see Rejected.)
175.

 # View Design: `arch::x86::mem::paging::table`
 
 ## Abstract Resource
 
 To callers this module is **a single hardware page-table page**: a fixed-length
 array of `PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH` (= 1024) typed entries, addressed by a *validated*
 in-range index (`TableIndex`) and backed by volatile, caller-owned memory at a
 physical/identity-mapped base address.
 
 Abstractly it is a **partial map `index → Option<E>`** over one page, plus two
 pure helpers (`pd_index`, `pt_index`) that extract the directory/table index of
 a virtual address. The phantom type `E` keeps PD and PT pages from being mixed.
 
 Two types need abstraction:
 
 | Type | What it is to a caller |
 |------|------------------------|
 | `TableIndex` | a *validated* slot number, guaranteed `< PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH` |
 | `Table<E>` | a typed, non-owning handle whose observable content is the per-slot entry map |
 
 ---
 
 ## View Structs
 
 ### `TableIndex`
 
 A `TableIndex` carries exactly one piece of caller-visible information: the
 validated index value. Its abstract value is a single `nat`.
 
 ```rust
 impl View for TableIndex {
     type V = nat;
     // value returned by into_raw(); always < PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH (see inv)
     pub closed spec fn view(&self) -> nat;
 }
 ```
 
 ### `Table<E>`
 
 ```rust
 pub struct TableView<E: TableEntry> {
     /// Physical/identity-mapped base address this handle denotes.
     /// Caller-meaningful identity: which page read/write act on.
     pub addr: nat,
     /// Logical contents: the entry a `read` would return for each valid slot.
     /// `entries[i] == None` means slot `i` holds a word that is not a valid
     /// encoding of `E`; `Some(e)` (including a not-present, zeroed entry) is a
     /// valid decode.
     pub entries: Map<nat, Option<E>>,
 }
 
 impl View for Table<E> {
     type V = TableView<E>;
     pub closed spec fn view(&self) -> TableView<E>;
 }
 ```
 
 `E: TableEntry` is `Copy`; the trait supplies two pure spec projections used by
 the transitions below (their `requires`/`ensures` are designed in the spec
 phase; `raw`/`from_raw` are in verification scope, so these are *proven*, not
 assumed):
 
 ```rust
 spec fn spec_raw(self: E) -> PteWord;              // serialize
 spec fn spec_from_raw(w: PteWord) -> Option<E>;    // decode (None = invalid)
 ```
 
 with the round-trip **trait law** `spec_from_raw(e.spec_raw()) == Some(e)`.
 
 ---
 
 ## Well-formedness Invariants
 
 ```rust
 // TableIndex: the validated-range guarantee callers depend on.
 pub open spec fn inv(&self) -> bool {     // on TableIndex
     self@ < PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH
 }
 ```
 
 ```rust
 impl<E: TableEntry> TableView<E> {
     pub open spec fn inv(self) -> bool {
         // exactly one page worth of slots, no more, no fewer
         &&& self.entries.dom() =~= Set::new(|i: nat| i < PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH)
         // a page-table page is page-aligned
         &&& self.addr % PAGE_SIZE == 0
     }
 }
 ```
 
 The `Table` type-level `inv()` is `self@.inv()`.
 
 ---
 
 ## Spec Transition Functions
 
 ### Pure index extractors (produce a `TableIndex` value = `nat`)
 
 ```rust
 pub open spec fn spec_table_index(vaddr: nat, shift: nat) -> nat {
     (vaddr >> shift) & (PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH - 1)        // low 10 bits after shift
 }
 pub open spec fn spec_pd_index(vaddr: nat) -> nat { spec_table_index(vaddr, PGTAB_SHIFT) }
 pub open spec fn spec_pt_index(vaddr: nat) -> nat { spec_table_index(vaddr, PAGE_SHIFT) }
 ```
 
 - `pd_index(vaddr)` → `result@ == spec_pd_index(vaddr as nat)` (and `inv`, i.e.
   `result@ < PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH`, which follows from the mask).
 - `pt_index(vaddr)` → `result@ == spec_pt_index(vaddr as nat)` (and `inv`).
 - `TableIndex::into_raw(self)` → `result == self@` (identity projection).
 - `TableIndex::new(i)` → `Some(t)` iff `i < PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH`, and then
   `t@ == i`; `None` otherwise. *(out of stated scope, but specifiable.)*
 
 ### Handle creation
 
 ```rust
 // from_address only fixes identity; contents are pre-existing memory.
 pub open spec fn spec_from_address(base: nat) -> /* addr field of */ nat { base }
 ```
 
 - `Table::from_address(base)` → `result@.addr == base`. `entries` are left
   unconstrained: they reflect whatever the backing page already holds.
 
 ### Read / write (the `index → Option<E>` map)
 
 ```rust
 impl<E: TableEntry> TableView<E> {
     pub open spec fn spec_read(self, idx: nat) -> Option<E> {
         self.entries[idx]
     }
     pub open spec fn spec_write(self, idx: nat, entry: E) -> TableView<E> {
         TableView {
             entries: self.entries.insert(idx, E::spec_from_raw(entry.spec_raw())),
             ..self                              // frame: addr unchanged
         }
     }
 }
 ```
 
 - `Table::read(&self, index)` → `result == self@.spec_read(index@)`
   (requires `index@ < PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH`, met by `TableIndex::inv`).
 - `Table::write(&self, index, entry)` →
   `self@ == old(self)@.spec_write(index@, entry)` — only slot `index@` changes,
   `addr` and every other slot are preserved by `..self` / `insert`.
 
 **Read-after-write** falls out directly:
 `spec_read(spec_write(s, i, e), i) == spec_from_raw(e.spec_raw())`, and by the
 trait round-trip law this is `Some(e)`. Writes to `j != i` leave slot `i`
 untouched because `Map::insert` only alters the keyed slot.
 
 ---
 
 ## Design Rationale (per field, with substitution test)
 
 > Substitution test: *if the implementation were rewritten with a different
 > algorithm, would this field still make sense?*
 
 ### `TableIndex@ : nat`
 - **Why:** the only thing every caller asks of a `TableIndex` is its numeric
   value and the promise it is `< PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH`. `gva.rs` does
   `into_raw().checked_mul(entry_size)` relying on that bound; `identity_map.rs`
   feeds it straight to `read`/`write`.
 - **Substitution:** ✅ Any representation (newtype over `usize`, a `u16`, a
   bitfield slice) still denotes one index value. `nat` is the algorithm-free
   essence; `into_raw` is its identity projection.
 
 ### `TableView::addr : nat`
 - **Why:** `from_address` has no other observable contract than *“this handle
   denotes the page at `base`.”* Callers build PD/PT handles from physical
   addresses they computed and must know the handle refers to that page.
 - **Substitution:** ✅ Any handle to a page-table page must know which page it
   addresses, regardless of how it stores it. (The `PhantomData` marker, by
   contrast, is pure implementation and is excluded — see Rejected.)
 
 ### `TableView::entries : Map<nat, Option<E>>`
 - **Why:** the read/write round-trip is the central thing callers reason about
   (caller analysis: *“model a table as a finite map `TableIndex → Option<E>`”*).
   `Option<E>` is exactly the read result: `None` = structurally invalid word
   (→ `InvalidArgument` at the call site), `Some(e)` = a valid entry, *including*
   a zeroed not-present entry.
 - **Substitution:** ✅ Whether the page is read volatilely word-by-word, via DMA,
   or copied wholesale, its observable state is still “what entry sits in each
   slot.” The map domain `[0, PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH)` is a hardware fact, not an
   implementation choice.
 - **Why `Option<E>` and not raw `PteWord`:** callers never reason in raw words;
   they consume `Option<E>`. Storing the decoded value keeps `spec_read` a
   trivial lookup (directly usable in caller proofs) and confines the
   `raw`/`from_raw` codec to a single place: `spec_write`.
 
 ### Why decode at *write* time in `spec_write`
 - Memory is static between a write and a later read, so decoding may be modeled
   at either end. Decoding at write (`from_raw(entry.raw())`) makes `spec_read` a
   pure map lookup and exposes the entry-codec round-trip as one clean obligation
   on the `E` trait — matching the documented trait expectation — rather than
   smearing `from_raw` across every read site.
 
 ---
 
 ## Rejected Alternatives
 
 - **Mirror the struct: `TableView { base: usize, _marker: PhantomData<E> }`.**
   Rejected — fails substitution and the caller-only test. `base`-as-`usize` and
   `PhantomData` are *how* the handle is built, not *what* callers observe; this
   View cannot express the read/write round-trip the identity map depends on
   (precisely the weakness called out for the current opaque placeholder).
 
 - **`entries : Map<nat, PteWord>` (raw words instead of decoded).**
   Rejected as the primary shape — faithful but forces `spec_read` to carry a
   `from_raw` on every lookup and pushes raw-word reasoning onto callers who only
   care about `Option<E>`. Kept in mind as an equivalent lower-level model; the
   decoded map is strictly friendlier for caller proofs.
 
 - **`entries : Seq<Option<E>>` (length-1024 sequence).**
   Rejected — a `Seq` ties the abstraction to dense 0..1024 indexing and makes
   per-slot frame conditions noisier (`forall j != i`). `Map` + `insert` gives a
   one-line frame condition and matches the “partial map” mental model.
 
 - **`spec_write` stores `Some(entry)` directly.**
   Rejected — unfaithful for any `E` whose encoding is lossy; it would silently
   assume the round-trip law instead of letting it discharge the read-back. The
   `from_raw(entry.raw())` form is faithful unconditionally and reduces to
   `Some(entry)` *only* via the explicit trait law.
 
 - **Encode the volatile-mechanism / `<< PTE_WORD_SIZE_LOG2` offset in the View.**
   Rejected — pure HOW. Callers explicitly don’t care (caller analysis); the
   byte offset is an addressing detail below the abstraction boundary.
 
 - **A separate `addr`-only `Table` View with contents threaded elsewhere.**
   Considered for the volatile-memory issue below; rejected for the *shape*
   because the deliverable’s transitions (`read`/`write`) need the contents map
   to live in one abstraction. The realization concern is handled at the spec
   layer (next note), not by weakening the View.
 
 ---
 
 ## Open Mechanism Note (for the spec phase, not a View-shape decision)
 
 `read`/`write` take `&self`, yet `write` must change `self@.entries`. The
 contents live in volatile, caller-owned memory, not inside the `Table` struct
 (which holds only `base`), so `Table::view()` cannot be a pure function of the
 struct alone, and two handles with equal `base` alias the same page.
 
 This does **not** change the View *shape*; it is a realization detail: the
 `entries` map will be carried by a ghost memory-permission token (PointsTo-style)
 threaded through `read`/`write` at the spec layer, keyed by `addr`. Recorded
 here so the specification phase wires `self@.entries` to that permission rather

6. # Verus Constraints
7. 
8. ## Attribute Style for Exec Functions
9. 
10. All specs on **exec functions** must use the attribute-based syntax
11. (`#[verus_spec]`, `#[verus_verify]`, `proof! { }`, `proof_decl! { }`).
12. See the **verus-syntax** skill for the full reference and examples.
13. 
14. ```rust
15. // ✅ CORRECT — attribute style for exec functions
16. #[verus_spec(ret =>
17.     requires x < 100,
18.     ensures ret == x + 1,
19. )]
20. fn foo(x: u32) -> u32 {
21.     x + 1
22. }
23. 
24. // ❌ WRONG — do not wrap exec functions in verus! { }
25. verus! {
26.     fn foo(x: u32) -> (ret: u32)
27.         requires x < 100,
28.         ensures ret == x + 1,
29.     { x + 1 }
30. } // verus!
31. ```
32. 
33. **`verus! { }` blocks** are still used for:
34. - `spec fn` and `proof fn` definitions (in `.spec.rs` and `.proof.rs`)
35. - Type-level specs (`broadcast`, `impl View`, etc.)
36.

38. signature is untouched, specs live in the attribute.

40. ## Source Integrity (exec code)
41. 
42. The following rules apply to the original source files (e.g. `lib.rs`), not to
43. `*.spec.rs` / `*.proof.rs` which are freely editable.
44. 
45. Verus verification is **in-place**: specs and proofs are added directly alongside
46. exec code. The annotated code remains fully compilable and runnable — Verus
47. constructs are erased during normal `cargo build` via cfg-gating. Keep changes
48. minimal so developers can review diffs easily.
49. 
50. **Preserve by default:** exec logic, function signatures, struct definitions,
51. comments, debug assertions, and all other existing code.
52. 
53. The escalation ladder (each step requires exhausting the previous):
54. 
55. 1. **Verify as-is** — most code works with Verus directly.
56. 2. **Search vstd** — your training data is likely outdated. `grep -r` the entire
57.    vstd directory broadly (see "vstd & Common Misconceptions" section below).
58. 3. If verification still fails after steps 1–2, try different proof
59.    strategies (add lemmas, intermediate assertions, split into smaller
60.    functions). If Verus reports that a **syntax construct is unsupported**
61.    (not a proof failure and not a missing spec for a stdlib function),
62.    record it in `verus-unsupported.md` with the exact error message and
63.    the minimal code that triggers it. Do NOT rewrite exec code, add
64.    `external_body`, or add `assume_specification` to work around it.
65. 
66. **The exec code has been pre-refactored to be fully compatible with Verus.**
67. There are no known Verus front-end limitations in the codebase. Any
68. verification failure is a proof issue, not a Verus limitation. Do NOT
69. rewrite exec code, add `external_body` — these are never needed.
70. 
71. **Never cfg-gate away and duplicate exec definitions.** Adding
72. `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` to a function, impl block, struct, enum, or
73. constant and providing a verus-annotated copy is forbidden — it verifies the
74. copy, not the real code, and the two will silently diverge.
75. 
76. - **Functions / impl blocks**: add contracts to the original in-place.
77. - **Structs / enums**: Verus sees the original definition directly. If a
78.   derive macro is incompatible, cfg-gate only the derive attribute, not
79.   the struct. If the struct truly cannot be parsed by Verus, use
80.   `external_type_specification` in spec.rs to declare it — do not
81.   duplicate the definition. Write `external_type_specification` **once**
82.   in the crate/module that defines the type; other modules `use` it.
83. - **Constants**: Verus sees the original definition directly. If Verus
84.   cannot resolve a constant from another workspace module, add
85.   `#[verus_verify]` to the defining module. Never
86.   `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` the original constant.
87. 
88. **Allowed additions:** `#[verus_spec(...)]` and `#[verus_verify]` attributes,
89. `proof! { }` / `proof_decl! { }` / `proof_with! { }` macros, `#[verus_spec(...)]`
90. on loops, `verus! { }` blocks (for spec/proof fn in .spec.rs/.proof.rs),
91. vstd imports (cfg-gated), ghost/tracked local variables (each must be
92. used by at least one proof construct — assertion, invariant, or proof block),
93. `Ghost<T>` / `Tracked<T>` struct fields (only when proof requires ghost
94. state to flow through exec code — prefer keeping ghost state in View),
95. `#[cfg_attr(not(verus_keep_ghost), derive(...))]` gating.
96. 
97. **After completing all changes**, use the `ast-consistency` skill to verify
98. source integrity. Fix all inconsistencies.

100. ## Forbidden Patterns
101. 
102. | Pattern | Policy |
103. |---|---|
104. | `admit()` | Allowed during specification phase as a placeholder. Must be eliminated during proving phase |
105. | `assume(...)` | Banned |
106. | `#[verifier::external_body]` | **On current module's own functions**: unconditionally forbidden in all phases — `admit()` in a proof body is the correct placeholder during specification (it skips only the proof obligation while Verus still checks exec code; `external_body` skips everything). **On dependency functions in other modules**: allowed as a temporary contract placeholder while the dependency is not yet verified. 107. | `#[verifier::trusted]` | Banned |
108. | `#[verifier::external]` | Banned — not needed under attribute style (only `#[verus_verify]`-annotated items are checked) |
109. | `#[verifier::exec_allows_no_decreases_clause]` | Banned |
110. | `#[verifier::spinoff_prover]` | Banned — even if verification passes with spinoff, the proof is fragile and will break with minor changes. Improve the proof itself |
111. | `#[verifier::rlimit(N)]` | Timeout means the proof is too weak — simplify the proof, split lemmas, add intermediate assertions. Never use rlimit to work around timeouts. If all proof strategies are exhausted and the proof is genuinely optimal, rlimit up to 50 is the absolute maximum |

113. | `uninterp spec fn` | **Banned** — all spec functions must have concrete definitions. Using `uninterp` to avoid writing a concrete spec is cheating — it has the same effect as `assume` when paired with `external_body` proof axioms |
114. 
115. ## cfg_attr and verus_keep_ghost
116. 
117. - **Do NOT wrap any Verus attribute or proof macro in `cfg_attr(verus_keep_ghost, ...)`, and do NOT guard one with `#[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]`.** This applies to `#[verus_spec(...)]`, `#[verus_verify(...)]`, `proof! { }`, `proof_decl! { }`, and `proof_with! { }`. 118. - **`use vstd::prelude::*;` must NOT be cfg-gated** — do not add `#[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]`. This import must be unconditionally present so that Verus-specific constructs (e.g. `#[verus_spec]`, `proof!{}`) are properly parsed and erased during normal `cargo build`.
119. 
120. See **verus-syntax** skill for correct examples.
121. 
122. ## Warnings
123. 
124. Verus verification must produce **zero warnings**. Two most common:
125. 
126. - **Missing trigger** — add `#[trigger]` on the relevant expression inside
127.   the quantifier, or annotate the quantifier with `#[auto]` to let Verus
128.   choose triggers automatically.
129. - **Incompatible derive** — `#[cfg_attr(not(verus_keep_ghost), derive(Clone, Debug, ...))]`
130.   to gate out derives that Verus cannot process.
131. 
132. ## Trust Boundaries (pre-approved TCB)
133. 
134. Trust boundaries — calls to code outside the verification scope whose
135. implementation cannot be verified (hardware registers, inline assembly, MMIO,
136. FFI, std library internals, external systems) — are the external-bottom
137. boundary. Which functions are trusted is **fixed in advance** by the TCB allowed
138. list (`tcb-allowed.md`). Do NOT introduce, justify, or record new trust
139. boundaries during specification or proving: if a function is not already in the
140. TCB allowed list, it must be fully verified or eliminated.
141. 
142. Mechanisms that rely on the TCB (`assume_specification`, `external_body`,
143. `axiom`) are only permitted on functions already in the allowed list.
144. 
145. **Do NOT use trust to hide proof failures.** If a function cannot be verified
146. after exhausting all proof strategies but is not in the TCB allowed list,
147. record it in `verification-todo.md` (in the logs directory) instead:
148. 
149. ```markdown
150. ## verification-todo.md entry format
151. - Function: `Foo::bar` (file.rs:42)
152. - Status: UNPROVEN
153. - Attempts: (list strategies tried)
154. - Blocker: (describe why verification fails)
155. ```
156. 
157. These are tracked separately so they are never mistaken for accepted trust
158. assumptions. The goal is to return and resolve them — not to accept them.
159. 
160. Recording a function here does **not** make verification pass: the cheating
161. gate ignores `verification-todo.md`, and any remaining `admit()` / `assume()`
162. still fails the gate. This file is an honest hand-off of genuinely-stuck
163. proofs — never an escape hatch for giving up.
164. 
165. ## assume_specification
166. 
167. `assume_specification` provides specs for std library or external functions
168. whose body Verus cannot verify (because vstd does not include them).
169. These are **external-bottom** trust assumptions (see **spec-design** skill) —
170. unverified axioms that, if wrong, make downstream proofs unsound.
171. 
172. **Allowed** for std library / external functions not covered by vstd.
173. Follow the audit checklist in `spec-design` (documentation fidelity, soft
174. contract coverage, no stronger than the API, version sensitivity).
175. 
176. **Before writing:** search vstd for existing specs of that function,
177. search verified dependency specs for reusable `assume_specification`,
178. look for safe Verus API alternatives, try restructuring to avoid the call.

181.

183. **Your training data is likely outdated.** Before concluding that a std
184. function has no spec or that a construct is unsupported, you **must** search
185. the actual vstd source thoroughly:

187. ```bash

193. two files. Look in `vstd/std_specs/`, `vstd/seq*.rs`, `vstd/map*.rs`,
194. `vstd/set*.rs`, `vstd/arithmetic/`, `vstd/raw_ptr.rs`, etc.
195. 
196. - **Never invent vstd functions** — verify existence in actual vstd source.
197. - **Verus supports `for` loops** — do not replace with `while` unless semantically appropriate.
198. - **Don't hallucinate syntax** — when unsure, check the Verus reference or vstd examples.
199.

201. 
202. **The exec code has been pre-refactored to be fully Verus-compatible.**
203. There are no known Verus front-end limitations in the codebase. Do NOT
204. claim any construct is unsupported, rewrite exec code, add `external_body`,
205. or use `// VERUS REWRITE`. Any verification failure is a proof issue —
206. strengthen the proof, do not change the code.
207.

211. appropriate for non-semantic items that Verus truly cannot parse:
212. `derive(Debug)`, `debug_assert!`, logging macros (`info!`, `error!`).
213. Do NOT cfg-gate match arms, closures, large code blocks, or expressions.
214. This makes Verus verify different code than what actually runs.
215. 
216. **Anti-pattern — body duplication (absolutely forbidden):**
217. 
218. ```rust
219. // ❌ WRONG: real body hidden from Verus, replaced with different code
220. fn foo(&mut self, x: usize) -> Result<(), Error> {
221.     #[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]
222.     { /* real implementation */ }
223.     #[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
224.     { /* different code that Verus can parse */ }
225. }
226. ```
227. 
228. **Anti-pattern — function duplication (absolutely forbidden):**
229. 
230. ```rust
231. // ❌ WRONG: entire function gated out, replaced with a different definition
232. #[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]
233. fn foo(&mut self, x: usize) -> Result<(), Error> { /* real */ }
234. #[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
235. fn foo(&mut self, x: usize) -> Result<(), Error> { /* different */ }
236. ```
237. 
238. Both patterns verify a **different program** than what ships. The proof is
239. meaningless. Find a single body that both Rust and Verus accept.

3. description: "Determine function-level verification order within a module using the verification plan. Use at the start of proving to know which function to verify first and how to sequence work."
4. ---
5. 
6. # Verification Order
7. 
8. ## Purpose
9. 
10. When proving a module, you must verify functions in **dependency order**:
11. verify callees before callers. This avoids wasting effort on callers whose
12. callees don't yet have specs, and ensures each function's dependencies are
13. already proven when you reach it.
14. 
15. ## How to Get the Order
16. 
17. A pre-generated verification plan may exist at:
18. 
19. ```
20. {logs_dir}/verification-plan.json
21. ```
22. 
23. If this file exists, use `show_fn_order.py` to display the function order:
24. 
25. ```bash
26. # Show function order for a specific module
27. python3 {scripts_dir}/show_fn_order.py {logs_dir}/verification-plan.json \
28.     -m "kernel::mm::phys::kpool"
29. 
30. # Glob pattern to match multiple modules
31. python3 {scripts_dir}/show_fn_order.py {logs_dir}/verification-plan.json \
32.     -m "bitmap::*"
33. ```
34. 
35. If the file does not exist, skip this step and use your best judgment for
36. function ordering (generally: leaf helpers first, public API functions last).
37. 
38. ## How to Use the Order
39. 
40. 1. **At the start of proving**, check for the plan and run `show_fn_order.py`.
41. 2. **Verify functions in the listed order** (top to bottom = leaves first).
42.    The first function has no intra-module dependencies; later functions
43.    may call earlier ones.
44. 3. **Do not skip ahead.** Resolve each function's `admit()` before moving
45.    to the next. This mirrors the proving-guide's "one function at a time"
46.    rule but with a concrete ordering.
47. 4. **Cross-module deps** listed in the output tell you which dependency
48.    modules need specs. If a callee in another module lacks a spec, write
49.    an `assume_specification` or verify that module first.
50. 
51. ## Output Format
52. 
53. ```
54. ## kernel::mm::phys::kpool
55.    crate: kernel  |  file: src/kernel/src/mm/phys/kpool.rs
56. 
57.     #  Function                        Line  In-module deps
58.   ───  ──────────────────────────────  ─────  ──────────────────────────────
59.     1  KpoolInner::alloc               L56   —
60.     2  KernelFrame::deref_mut          L160  —
61.     3  KernelFrame::clear              L144  KernelFrame::deref_mut
62.     4  Kpool::alloc                    L205  KpoolInner::alloc, clear
63. ```
64. 
65. Use `-v` to also see cross-module dependency modules.
66. 
67. Functions are ordered so that by the time you reach function N, all its
68. intra-module dependencies (functions 1..N-1) are already verified.
69.

 ## Purpose
 
 When proving a module, you must verify functions in **dependency order**:

 already proven when you reach it.
 
 ## How to Get the Order

 ```bash
     -m "bitmap::*"
 ```
 
 If the file does not exist, skip this step and use your best judgment for
 function ordering (generally: leaf helpers first, public API functions last).
 
 ## How to Use the Order
 
 1. **At the start of proving**, check for the plan and run `show_fn_order.py`.
 2. **Verify functions in the listed order** (top to bottom = leaves first).
    The first function has no intra-module dependencies; later functions
    may call earlier ones.
 3. **Do not skip ahead.** Resolve each function's `admit()` before moving
    to the next. This mirrors the proving-guide's "one function at a time"
    rule but with a concrete ordering.
 4. **Cross-module deps** listed in the output tell you which dependency
    modules need specs. If a callee in another module lacks a spec, write
    an `assume_specification` or verify that module first.
 
 ## Output Format
 
 ```

     4  Kpool::alloc                    L205  KpoolInner::alloc, clear
 ```

 Functions are ordered so that by the time you reach function N, all its
 intra-module dependencies (functions 1..N-1) are already verified.

data.deltaContent: I
'm looking at how the identity_map.spec.rs module declares external specifications
for the Table type and its associated methods, and now I need
to check whether the table module itself has any conflicting definitions with what's already
been registered upstream.
The
key issue is that identity_map.spec.rs uses `assume_specification` for functions like `pd_index`, `pt_index`, and
the Table methods with no requires/ensures clauses, treating them as opaque.
If I add real Verus specs to these same functions in the arch crate, that creates a conflict since `
assume_specification` is meant for functions without specs. The constraint is that I can
't weaken or remove existing ensures/requires from upstream modules—I need to reference the existing specs rather
than redefine them.
So
the real tension is that if I add proper
specs to the table module, the kernel's identity_map.spec.rs will have conflicting external
specs and assume_specification placeholders. The task says to remove those
when the dependency is verified, but also says not to touch unlisted functions. My
priority should be getting `make verify-arch` to pass cleanly first, then address

any `make verify` regressions from the identity_map conflict.

The bigger challenge is designing the
View for Table when the entries map lives in volatile memory outside the struct itself. The struct
only holds the base address, so a pure view() can only expose that. I need to think about
whether the entries map should be modeled as a separate ghost permission token threaded through read/write operations, or if there
's a simpler approach that works with the exec signatures as they are.
I
'm realizing that adding a requires clause to `from_address` would force `
identity_map` callers to prove alignment, which breaks the existing proof even though the bodies use `admit()`. The
core issue is that I can't thread a permission token through the existing `&self` signatures without changing them, and ghost fields
won't help since `read`/`write` only have
immutable access. I need to step back and think about what
's actually feasible at the spec phase with `admit()` bodies —
maybe using an uninterpreted global per address, though that's restricted
, or reconsidering whether adding a ghost field to the struct is viable
despite the aliasing issues with shared memory.
The
achievable specs are the pure functions like `pd_index`, `pt_index`, and `TableIndex::into
_raw` which can fully specify their results, while `read` and `write` hit a
wall because expressing the round-trip mutation requires either a mutable reference or a ghost permission token that we
can't add without changing signatures. For `from_address` I
can specify the address constraint, and I should probably spec
`TableIndex::new` too since it's listed in scope and helps establish invariants.
The real question is whether the View itself needs reconsidering to
handle the volatile memory semantics.

ine how the repo handles pointer/volatile memory in verified specs and the build/verify setup.

# Verifies all Verus-annotated crates.
.PHONY: verify $(addprefix verify-,$(VERUS_CRATES))
verify: $(addprefix verify-,$(VERUS_CRATES)) verify-kernel

# Ensures the correct Verus version is installed before verification.
# When VERUS_EXECUTABLE_DIR is unset, verification is skipped.
# When set, validates that the verus binary exists at the given path.
.PHONY: ensure-verus
ensure-verus:
ifeq ($(VERUS_EXECUTABLE_DIR),)
	@echo "VERUS_EXECUTABLE_DIR is not set; skipping verification."
else
	@verus_dir="$(VERUS_EXECUTABLE_DIR)"; \
	if command -v cygpath >/dev/null 2>&1; then \
		verus_dir="$$(cygpath -u "$$verus_dir")"; \
	fi; \
	verus_path="$$verus_dir/$(VERUS_BINARY)"; \
	if [ ! -f "$$verus_path" ]; then \
		echo "Error: VERUS_EXECUTABLE_DIR is set to '$(VERUS_EXECUTABLE_DIR)' but no $(VERUS_BINARY) found there."; \
		exit 1; \
	fi; \
	if [ "$(IS_WINDOWS)" != "yes" ] && [ ! -x "$$verus_path" ]; then \
		echo "Error: $(VERUS_BINARY) at '$$verus_path' is not executable."; \
		exit 1; \
	fi; \
	echo "Using Verus installation at $(VERUS_EXECUTABLE_DIR)."
endif

# Pattern rule for verifying individual crates.
# Verification is skipped when VERUS_EXECUTABLE_DIR is unset.
$(addprefix verify-,$(VERUS_CRATES)): verify-%: ensure-verus
ifeq ($(VERUS_EXECUTABLE_DIR),)
	@true
else
	RUSTFLAGS=$(KERNEL_RUST_FLAGS) \
	PATH="$(VERUS_PATH_PREFIX):$$PATH" \
	VERUS_AI_DIR="$(VERUS_AI_DIR)" \
	VERUS_EXTRA_CARGO_ARGS="--locked $(KERNEL_CARGO_FLAGS) $(KERNEL_CARGO_TARGET)" \
	$(VERUS_AI_VERIFY_SCRIPT) --crate $* $(VERUS_MODULE_ARG) --log-dir verus-ai-logs/verify-$*
endif

# Verifies all Verus-annotated crates.
.PHONY: verify $(addprefix verify-,$(VERUS_CRATES))
verify: $(addprefix verify-,$(VERUS_CRATES)) verify-kernel

# Ensures the correct Verus version is installed before verification.
# When VERUS_EXECUTABLE_DIR is unset, verification is skipped.
# When set, validates that the verus binary exists at the given path.
.PHONY: ensure-verus
ensure-verus:
ifeq ($(VERUS_EXECUTABLE_DIR),)
	@echo "VERUS_EXECUTABLE_DIR is not set; skipping verification."
else
	@verus_dir="$(VERUS_EXECUTABLE_DIR)"; \
	if command -v cygpath >/dev/null 2>&1; then \
		verus_dir="$$(cygpath -u "$$verus_dir")"; \
	fi; \
	verus_path="$$verus_dir/$(VERUS_BINARY)"; \
	if [ ! -f "$$verus_path" ]; then \
		echo "Error: VERUS_EXECUTABLE_DIR is set to '$(VERUS_EXECUTABLE_DIR)' but no $(VERUS_BINARY) found there."; \
		exit 1; \
	fi; \
	if [ "$(IS_WINDOWS)" != "yes" ] && [ ! -x "$$verus_path" ]; then \
		echo "Error: $(VERUS_BINARY) at '$$verus_path' is not executable."; \
		exit 1; \
	fi; \
	echo "Using Verus installation at $(VERUS_EXECUTABLE_DIR)."
endif

# Pattern rule for verifying individual crates.
# Verification is skipped when VERUS_EXECUTABLE_DIR is unset.
$(addprefix verify-,$(VERUS_CRATES)): verify-%: ensure-verus
ifeq ($(VERUS_EXECUTABLE_DIR),)
	@true
else
	RUSTFLAGS=$(KERNEL_RUST_FLAGS) \
	PATH="$(VERUS_PATH_PREFIX):$$PATH" \
	VERUS_AI_DIR="$(VERUS_AI_DIR)" \

	$(VERUS_AI_VERIFY_SCRIPT) --crate $* $(VERUS_MODULE_ARG) --log-dir verus-ai-logs/verify-$*
endif

# Plan: Verus specs for arch::x86::mem::paging::table

## Scope functions
Table::write, TableIndex::into_raw, raw, Table::read, from_raw, pt_index,
TableIndex, pd_index, Table::from_address

## View design (from view_design.md)
- TableIndex@ : nat, inv = @ < PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH (type_invariant)
- Table<E>@   : addr (nat) [+ entries via permission — deferred]
- TableEntry: spec_raw / spec_from_raw projections + round-trip law

## Phases
1. [done] Read context, skills, baseline verify-arch (8 verified, 0 errors).
2. Pure index funcs: pd_index, pt_index, TableIndex::new, into_raw — full specs.
3. from_address: ensures result@ == base.
4. raw/from_raw trait projections + round-trip law.
5. read/write: contracts over View transitions; volatile mem handling.
6. Run verify-arch -> 0 errors. Then verify (regressions) + build.

## Key tension / decisions
- write(&self) cannot mutate a pure struct-view -> entries need a perm token.
  view_design defers this to a PointsTo perm keyed by addr.
- Upstream kernel identity_map.spec.rs has external_type_specification +
  state-free assume_specification for Table/TableIndex/pd_index/pt_index/
  from_address/read/write. Real specs here will SUPERSEDE these -> must remove
  the now-redundant placeholders from identity_map.spec.rs to keep `make verify`
  green (methodology: placeholders removed when dependency module is verified).
- No external_body (not in tcb-allowed.md). No signature changes.
